newsitem.title: FINLAND: NEW HARMONISATION SEEN NOT CHANGING FINNISH CPI.
newsitem.headline: NEW HARMONISATION SEEN NOT CHANGING FINNISH CPI.

text.p: The next phase of harmonisation of European consumer price indexes will not bring major changes to the Finnish EU harmonised CPI, but the figure will rise this year due to other factors, Statistics Finland (SF) said on Wednesday.
"There will not be much difference between VYHKI and YHKI," SF senior statistician Arja Kinnunen told a seminar.
VYHKI is the Finnish abbreviation for the partly harmonised CPI figure and YHKI is the abbreviation for the index in use when the harmonisation reaches phase two.
The first new CPI figures will be published on March 7.

The European Union's statistics agency Eurostat is scheduled to release consumer price figures calculated according to the second harmonisation phase for all EU countries that day, Kinnunen said. January 1997 inflation data will be published.
"For the first time we will get really comparable information," she said.
The national baskets of consumer goods and methods of collecting price data to gauge inflation vary significantly in different EU countries, she noted.
The harmonised inflation figures will be used to determine which countries qualify for the third stage of EMU.

The EMU inflation criterion says that to qualify for membership of the single currency a country's annual rate of EU harmonised inflation must not exceed by more than 1.5 percentage points the mean pace of inflation of the three EU countries with the lowest annual rise in harmonised CPI.
The inflation reading is also a decisive factor for another EMU criterion -- long-term interest rates.

To be eligible for EMU a country's medium-term interest rates -- yields on government benchmark bonds -- must not exceed by more than two percentage points the mean of yields in the three EU countries with the slowest inflation.

Kirsi Hokka, economist at brokerage Alfred Berg, said she expected the year-on-year rise in the YHKI to be around two percent at the end of 1997. It was hard to predict whether Finland would be among the three pace-setting countries as quite many countries would be around 1.5-2.0 percent, she said.
But it was "quite clear" that Finnish EU harmonised inflation would be within 1.5 percentage points of the mean inflation of the three countries with the slowest CPI rise, Hokka said.
In December, Finland's partly harmonised CPI rose 1.5 percent year-on-year.
The year-on-year rise in the partly harmonised index had been constantly below 1.5 percent since February 1995.
The rise in Finnish consumer prices was likely to pick up speed slightly this year, Kinnunen said.
"The downward effect (on CPI) of falling food prices will come to an end soon," she said.
Food prices fell sharply in 1995-96 after Finland joined the European Union. The fall in food prices, and lower interest rates, made the CPI rise very subdued.
Now food prices have stabilised and the past price decline will soon no longer affect inflation, Kinnunen said.
--Peter Starck, Helsinki Newsroom +358 - 9 - 680 50 245
